{{short description|Canadian astronomer}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=January 2022}}
'''Dale A. Frail''' (b. 1961) is a Canadian [[astronomer]] working at the [[National Radio Astronomy Observatory]] (NRAO) in [[Socorro, New Mexico|Socorro]], [[New Mexico]].

==Early life==
He was born in [[Canada]], spent much of his childhood in [[Europe]], and his professional career has been based in the [[United States]].

==Career==

Frail received his university education in Canada: first an undergraduate degree in [[Physics]] from [[Acadia University]] in [[Nova Scotia]], followed by MSc and PhD degrees in [[Astrophysics]] from the [[University of Toronto]]. In 1989 he moved to the United States as an [[NSERC]] Postdoctoral Fellow. After completing a prized Jansky Postdoctoral Fellowship<ref>{{cite web |title=2026 Jansky Fellowship Program |url=https://science.nrao.edu/opportunities/postdoctoral-programs/jansky |publisher=National Radio Astronomy Observatory|accessdate=June 9, 2026}}</ref> in 1993, he joined the research staff of the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, where he remained throughout his career. He was awarded Astronomer Emeritus status by [[Associated Universities, Inc.]] upon retirement in 2021, and continues active research programs.

He is the author of over 250 peer-reviewed research papers,<ref>[http://adsabs.harvard.edu/cgi-bin/nph-abs_connect?db_key=AST&db_key=PRE&qform=AST&arxiv_sel=astro-ph&arxiv_sel=cond-mat&arxiv_sel=cs&arxiv_sel=gr-qc&arxiv_sel=hep-ex&arxiv_sel=hep-lat&arxiv_sel=hep-ph&arxiv_sel=hep-th&arxiv_sel=math&arxiv_sel=math-ph&arxiv_sel=nlin&arxiv_sel=nucl-ex&arxiv_sel=nucl-th&arxiv_sel=physics&arxiv_sel=quant-ph&arxiv_sel=q-bio&sim_query=YES&ned_query=YES&adsobj_query=YES&aut_logic=OR&obj_logic=OR&author=Frail%0D%0A&object=&start_mon=&start_year=&end_mon=&end_year=&ttl_logic=OR&title=&txt_logic=OR&text=&nr_to_return=300&start_nr=1&jou_pick=NO&ref_stems=&data_and=ALL&group_and=ALL&start_entry_day=&start_entry_mon=&start_entry_year=&end_entry_day=&end_entry_mon=&end_entry_year=&min_score=&sort=SCORE&data_type=SHORT&aut_syn=YES&ttl_syn=YES&txt_syn=YES&aut_wt=1.0&obj_wt=1.0&ttl_wt=0.3&txt_wt=3.0&aut_wgt=YES&obj_wgt=YES&ttl_wgt=YES&txt_wgt=YES&ttl_sco=YES&txt_sco=YES&version=1 "Dale Frail"], Partial list from the ''[[NASA]] [[Astrophysics Data System|ADS]]'' database</ref> including more than 30 articles in the prestigious journal [[Nature (journal)|Nature]]. He has made contributions to numerous sub-fields of astrophysics including multi-wavelength [[Electromagnetic_spectrum|electromagnetic]] counterparts of [[Gravitational-wave_astronomy|gravitational-wave events]], [[gamma-ray bursts]], [[extrasolar planets]], [[Soft gamma repeater|soft gamma-ray repeaters]], the [[interstellar medium]], [[pulsars]], [[Astrophysical maser|masers]], and [[supernova remnants]]. To the public he is best known for discoveries in extrasolar planets and gamma-ray bursts. In [[List of Guggenheim Fellowships awarded in 2010|2010]], he was awarded a [[Guggenheim fellowship]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gf.org/fellows/dale-a-frail/ |title=Dale Frail |publisher=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |accessdate=June 9, 2026}}</ref> From August 2011 through September 2015, he was NRAO's Assistant Director for the [[Karl G. Jansky]] [[Very Large Array]] and the [[Very Long Baseline Array]], and site director for New Mexico operations.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://science.nrao.edu/enews/4.6/index.shtml |title=New Assistant Director for EVLA, VLBA, and NM Ops Appointed |publisher=National Radio Astronomy Observatory eNews |date=June 14, 2011 |accessdate=June 9, 2026 }}</ref> In 2016, he received an honorary Doctor of Science degree from [[Acadia University]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www2.acadiau.ca/home/news-reader-page/convocation-2016-acadia-to-confer-six-honorary-degrees.html |title=Acadia to confer six honorary degrees during Convocation 2016 |date=May 12, 2016 |publisher=[[Acadia University]] |accessdate=June 9, 2026 |archive-date=May 18, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160518033722/https://www2.acadiau.ca/home/news-reader-page/convocation-2016-acadia-to-confer-six-honorary-degrees.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Key discoveries==

In early 1992, Frail and Polish astronomer [[Aleksander Wolszczan]] announced their discovery<ref>{{cite journal |  author=Wolszczan, A. |  author2=Frail, D. A. | title=A planetary system around the millisecond pulsar PSR1257+12 | journal=Nature | year=1992 | volume=355 | issue= 6356| pages=145&ndash;147 | doi=10.1038/355145a0 | bibcode=1992Natur.355..145W| s2cid=4260368 }}</ref> of the existence of two planets and a possible third around the pulsar [[PSR B1257+12]]. Their discovery was confirmed in mid-1992. In addition to being the first confirmed discovery of [[pulsar planets]], the find is also generally considered to be the first confirmed discovery of extrasolar planets of any kind.

Beginning in 1997, Frail was part of a [[Caltech]]-NRAO team that helped unravel the long-standing mystery of the origin of gamma-ray bursts. They used an optical spectrum taken with the [[Keck Telescope]] toward the optical afterglow of [[GRB 970508]] to establish that gamma-ray bursts were at [[cosmological distances]].<ref>{{cite journal | author=Metzger, M. R. | author2=Djorgovski, S. G. | author3=Kulkarni, S. R. | author4=Steidel, C. C. | author5=Adelberger, K. L. | author6=Frail, D. A. | author7=Costa, E. | author8=Frontera, F. | title=Spectral constraints on the redshift of the optical counterpart to the γ-ray burst of 8 May 1997 | journal=Nature | year=1997 | volume=387 | issue= 6636| pages=878&ndash;880 | bibcode=1997Natur.387..878M | doi=10.1038/43132| doi-access=free }}</ref> They then used the [[Very Large Array]] [[radio telescope]] discovery of radio afterglow emission from this same burst to measure the object's size and infer that the source was expanding relativistically.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Frail, D. A. | author2=Kulkarni, S. R. | author3=Nicastro, L. | author4=Feroci, M. | author5=Taylor, G. B. | title=The radio afterglow from the γ-ray burst of 8 May 1997 | journal=Nature | year=1997 | volume=389 | issue= 6648| pages=261&ndash;263 | bibcode=1997Natur.389..261F | doi=10.1038/38451| s2cid=4342265 }}</ref> These two observations have remained cornerstones in the cosmological fireball model for gamma-ray bursts.<ref>{{cite journal | author=Piran, T. | title=Gamma-ray bursts and the fireball model | journal=Physics Reports | volume=314 | issue= 6| pages=575&ndash;667 | year=1999 | arxiv=astro-ph/9810256 | doi=10.1016/S0370-1573(98)00127-6|bibcode = 1999PhR...314..575P | s2cid=118919707 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1086/309024 | author=Frail, D. A. | author2=Waxman, E. | author3=Kulkarni, S. R. | title=A 450 Day Light Curve of the Radio Afterglow of GRB 970508: Fireball Calorimetry | journal=The Astrophysical Journal | year=2000 | volume=537 | issue= 1| pages=191&ndash;204 | bibcode=2000ApJ...537..191F |arxiv = astro-ph/9910319 | s2cid=15652654 }}</ref> In 2009 Thomson ISI listed Frail as the third-most cited researcher in the field of gamma-ray bursts over the period from 1999 to February 2009.<ref>https://web.archive.org/web/20130414075034/http://archive.sciencewatch.com/ana/st/gamma/authors/ Special Topics Analysis of Gamma-ray Burst (GRB) Research</ref>

In 2026, the [[American Institute of Physics]] (AIP) published an article on the history of the pulsar planets discovery, based on interviews with Wolszczan and Frail.<ref>{{cite web |first=Rebecca |last=Charbonneau |title=New oral histories: The discovery of the first exoplanets |publication-date=May 29, 2026 |url=https://www.aip.org/history/new-oral-histories-the-discovery-of-the-first-exoplanets-may-29-2026 |access-date=June 9, 2026 }}</ref> There are many other popular science accounts of the discovery of extra-solar planets as well as those of gamma-ray bursts and their afterglows. Links to a few of these and other relevant articles can be found below.
